mcqs.question: A login form returns "invalid password" for a wrong password on an existing account, and a different, generic "account not found" message for a username that doesn't exist. What has this design leaked?
options: Whether a given username exists in the system, without the attacker needing to break anything else
The user's actual password, in plaintext
The database engine and version running behind the application
Nothing — differentiating the two error cases is a UX best practice with no security implication
mcqs.explanation: Differentiated responses let an attacker enumerate valid usernames just by observing which error comes back, which is real reconnaissance value even though no password or system detail is directly exposed. This isn't a UX-only concern, and neither the password nor the database engine is revealed by this specific behavior.

mcqs.question: A framework's debug mode is left enabled in production. What is the realistic consequence when an unhandled exception occurs?
options: Nothing user-visible changes since debug mode only affects local development servers
The application automatically shuts down to protect against exploitation
The exception is silently swallowed and no response is returned at all
A full stack trace, and sometimes source code snippets or local variable values, gets rendered directly to whoever triggered the exception
mcqs.explanation: Debug mode is designed to show exactly this level of detail to whoever sees the error page, and it doesn't stop working just because the deployment is production — that's precisely the risk. It doesn't shut the app down or silently swallow errors, and it absolutely does affect production servers if the flag is left on there.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of returning a correlation ID alongside a generic error message to the user?
options: It encrypts the error message so only the intended user can read it
It automatically retries the failed request on the user's behalf
It is required by law in most jurisdictions for any API error response
It lets an engineer look up the full, detailed internal log entry for that specific failure using the ID the user reports, without exposing that detail in the response itself
mcqs.explanation: The correlation ID bridges a safe, generic external response with the full internal log detail needed for debugging — support or engineering can find the exact failure by ID without the detail ever having left the system. It has nothing to do with encryption, doesn't trigger a retry, and isn't a general legal requirement.

mcqs.question: A login endpoint returns the identical error message for a wrong password and a nonexistent username, but responds noticeably slower for the wrong-password case. What can an attacker still learn?
options: Whether a given username exists, by measuring response time even though the message text gives nothing away
The exact password, from the response timing alone
The database's IP address
Nothing at all, since the message text is identical in both cases
mcqs.explanation: A timing side channel can distinguish two cases even when the visible output is identical — the slower response for an existing username, caused by an extra comparison step, reveals the username's existence through timing alone. It doesn't reveal the password itself or any network-level detail like an IP address, and the identical message text doesn't neutralize the timing leak.

mcqs.question: Why is inconsistency across endpoints, rather than one single dramatic mistake, described as the more realistic source of information leakage in a large codebase?
options: Because leakage only ever happens in exactly one endpoint per application
Because most frameworks make consistent error handling technically impossible
Because different teams or endpoints handling errors slightly differently means some fall back to safe defaults while others still leak detail, and no single fix closes every gap at once
Because inconsistent error handling always improves application performance
mcqs.explanation: With many endpoints and teams, safe error handling applied inconsistently leaves scattered gaps rather than one obvious hole — which is exactly why a shared, platform-level default (middleware every endpoint gets automatically) closes more of the gap than fixing endpoints one at a time. Leakage isn't confined to a single endpoint, frameworks don't prevent consistency, and inconsistency has no performance benefit.

mcqs.question: An API's catch-all error handler returns `{"error": str(exception)}` directly in the response body. What's the risk in this pattern?
options: It has no risk, since JSON responses cannot contain sensitive information by definition

It serializes the raw exception detail — potentially including internal paths, query fragments, or driver-specific messages — straight into a response that leaves the system, the same leak as leaving debug mode on
It will always cause the API to return a 500 status code regardless of the actual error
It prevents the exception from being logged internally at all
mcqs.explanation: Serializing an exception's string form directly into the response exposes exactly the kind of internal detail a safe error handler should keep server-side only — this is functionally the same leak as an enabled debug page, just inside a JSON API. JSON responses can absolutely carry sensitive data, the status code returned isn't fixed by this pattern, and it doesn't prevent separate internal logging (though relying on the response instead of a proper log is itself part of the problem).
